extracted.intended_audience: general readers and people interested in television production and Saturday Night Live
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural expectations for producing and structuring a live sketch-comedy/variety television episode in the style of Saturday Night Live, including episode format, cast and writer roles, production week workflow, technical/staging constraints, and music/photography policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode format and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: An SNL episode is a live sketch comedy/variety show that is hosted by a celebrity guest and features a musical guest; an episode normally begins with a cold open based on current events and ends with someone breaking character and proclaiming, "Live from New York, it's Saturday Night!" before credits and introduction of the guest host.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical components: cold open (topical), host monologue near start, sketches with cast and host, one or more musical performances, and closing line. The host usually delivers the monologue and performs in sketches. Follow this overall order when structuring an episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live broadcast and runtime expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: SNL is broadcast live with a studio audience; running time is 60–70 minutes (without commercials) and the show occupies a 93-minute timeslot beginning at 11:29:30 p.m. Eastern Time (with live broadcasts across the contiguous United States since 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the live aspect whenever possible — many production choices (no lip-syncing, live band, timing of rehearsals) support the program's live identity. Plan show length and content to fit the scheduled timeslot and live broadcast constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cold open topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: The cold open sketch is usually based on current political or pop cultural events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize topicality and immediacy for the cold open; produce and revise content late in the week to reflect current events. Cold opens often focus on political satire or recent pop-culture stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host responsibilities and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode is hosted by a celebrity guest who delivers the opening monologue, performs in sketches with the cast, and introduces the musical guest; the host usually ends the opening monologue by mentioning the musical guest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design material that fits the host's strengths and publicity cycle (films, albums). Hosts may participate in pitching ideas during Monday meetings and may be involved in sketch selection. The monologue is given low priority and can be finalized late in the week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekend Update segment standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Weekend Update is a segment featuring one or two hosts performing as themselves; it has a dedicated three- to four-member writing team, and the Update hosts normally do not work with or read the segment scripts until Thursday evening after main sketches are finalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Weekend Update as an internally distinct unit: maintain a small dedicated team, time the Update writing and host rehearsals later in the week, and understand that Update hosting is a high-profile role that provides substantial screen time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical guest policies (no lip-syncing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Michaels does not allow musical guests to perform using lip-synching tracks, believing it diminishes the live aspect of the show; exceptions are made only when the musical act is focused on intense dance routines instead of vocals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Book musical performances that can be performed live vocally; reserve lip-synching only when dance-heavy staging makes live singing impractical. Musical guests typically perform two or three numbers and may also serve as host.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast recruitment and tiering
rubrics_metrics.description: Cast members are normally recruited from improvisational comedy groups (The Groundlings, Second City, UCB, ImprovOlympic) or established stand-up comedians; the cast is divided into repertory players (established) and featured players (newer/unproven) who may eventually be promoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit performers with improv or stand-up backgrounds and experience; use the featured/repertory tier system to manage development and promotion of talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production week workflow and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Production normally starts Monday with a free-form pitch meeting; Tuesday is dedicated to writing (writing may not begin until 8:00 p.m.); Wednesday at 5:00 p.m. sketches are read in a round-table read-through; Thursday focuses on developing and rewriting sketches; Friday and Saturday are for rehearsals; Saturday includes a rehearsal before a live audience at 8:00 p.m. and the live broadcast that night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to the tight weekly cadence: pitch Monday, write Tuesday, read Wednesday, rewrite Thursday, rehearse Friday/Saturday. Expect late changes and plan staffing/scheduling accordingly. Host and guest availability constraints can compress photo/video and rehearsal schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch selection and decision-making authority
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Wednesday read-through, Michaels, the head writer, the guest host, and some producers decide the show's layout in Michaels's office and determine which sketches will be developed for air; once the writers and cast are shown the lineup they learn whether their sketch survived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that final sketch selection is centralized (showrunner and key producers). Present and polish ideas for the read-through with awareness that many sketches will be cut; prepare to revise or abandon sketches on short notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show length constraint and removal of sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: Michaels will review the show lineup to ensure it meets a 90-minute length, and sketches that have made it as far as the live rehearsal may be removed; this often results in less than two days of rehearsal for the sketches that make it to air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sketches with adaptability for duration and cut-ability; expect last-minute trims to satisfy length and pacing; rehearse for tight timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical feasibility assessment during read-through
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wednesday read-through is attended by writers, producers, and technical experts such as make-up artists who may be required to realize certain sketch ideas (e.g., prosthetics), resulting in roughly fifty people evaluating around forty sketch ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring technical concerns to the read-through: if an idea requires complicated makeup/props/costumes or video effects, involve technical staff early to assess feasibility and timeline implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and role of pre-recorded material
rubrics_metrics.description: SNL uses pre-recorded elements for certain commercial parodies, SNL Digital Shorts, and show graphics; pre-recorded material is processed off-site and in some eras has outshone live material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide strategically which pieces should be pre-recorded versus live; schedule off-site production time for shorts and ensure they integrate with the live show's timing. Pre-recorded elements can expand creative possibilities but require separate post-production resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehearsal time limitations and staffing implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the show's development and cutting process, the final sketches that make it to air often receive less than two full days of rehearsal for the eight to twelve sketches on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for condensed rehearsal schedules and prioritize blocking/technical run-throughs for sketches in the final lineup; consider simplified staging where necessary to accommodate limited rehearsal time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photography and promotional imagery aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Official SNL photographers (e.g., Mary Ellen Matthews) employ flattering portrait lighting with hard lights to achieve a Hollywood style, aiming for contrast and depth; host photos are attempted on Tuesday and musical guest photos on Thursday when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For promotional bumpers and stills, use high-contrast lighting and edge/background lighting to create depth; schedule quick on-site shoots early in the production week given host/musical-guest availability constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical production equipment standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Studio 8H uses industry-standard broadcast equipment (as of the article: five Sony HDC-1500 cameras, Vinten pedestals, a Chapman-Leonard Electra crane, Grass Valley routing/switchers, Chyron and Avid graphics, Calrec and Yamaha audio consoles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan camera blocking, graphics, and audio workflows around the studio's equipment capabilities; use appropriate technical staff to integrate multi-camera live switching, on-set graphics, and broadcast audio mixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast contract and career mobility provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 1999–2000, new hires were tied to a rewritten contract allowing NBC to place a cast member in an NBC sitcom (cast members can reject the first two sitcom offers but must accept the third; the contract also optioned cast members for feature films and allowed NBC a network option to remove a cast member at any time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat casting decisions and career planning with awareness of contractual obligations and network options; both performers and agents should consider long-term implications when accepting employment.
